library(knitr)

```{r read_tables}
source("helpers_claude.R")
csv_dir <- "csv"
# A trial knit on small fits reads its tables from elsewhere.
if(Sys.getenv("GABITTO_OUT_DIR") != ""){
  csv_dir <- file.path(Sys.getenv("GABITTO_OUT_DIR"), "csv")
}
.read <- function(name){
  utils::read.csv(file.path(csv_dir, name), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
donor_df <- utils::read.csv(file.path("csv", "split_donors.csv"),
                            stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
balance_df <- utils::read.csv(file.path("csv", "split_balance.csv"),
                              stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
fit_df <- .read("fits.csv")
agreement_df <- .read("agreement.csv")
discovery_df <- .read("discovery.csv")
cross_df <- .read("cross_score.csv")
summary_df <- .read("summary.csv")
run_df <- .read("rule_runs.csv")
pair_df <- .read("gene_pairs.csv.gz")
calls_df <- .read("esvd_calls.csv")

split_vec <- c("split1", "split2")
method_vec <- unique(summary_df$method)
rule_vec <- c("stored", "null_rescaled", "deshrunk", "raw", "raw_null",
              "donor_wls", "gap_trend", "embed_prior", "state_adjusted")
# The methods that get a subsection of their own: the nine rules as the
# loops ran them, the two unfloored variants the beyond-score study
# recommended, and DESeq2.
section_vec <- c(rule_vec, "donor_wls@esvd_nofloor",
                 "state_adjusted@esvd_nofloor", "deseq2")
stopifnot(all(section_vec %in% method_vec))

fmt <- function(x, digits = 2){formatC(x, digits = digits, format = "f")}
pct <- function(x, digits = 0){paste0(formatC(100 * x, digits = digits,
                                              format = "f"), "%")}
# One number of the summary table.
sm <- function(method, column, split){
  summary_df[summary_df$method == method & summary_df$split == split, column]
}
# The same number in the two splits, as "a and b".
both <- function(method, column, digits = 2, bool_pct = FALSE){
  value_vec <- sapply(split_vec, function(split){sm(method, column, split)})
  text_vec <- if(bool_pct) pct(value_vec) else fmt(value_vec, digits)
  paste0(text_vec[1], " and ", text_vec[2])
}
# One number of the agreement table.
ag <- function(method, gene_set, column, split){
  agreement_df[agreement_df$method == method & agreement_df$split == split &
                 agreement_df$gene_set == gene_set, column]
}
# The mean of a summary column over the two splits, for ranking.
avg <- function(column){
  value_vec <- tapply(summary_df[[column]], summary_df$method, mean)
  value_vec[method_vec]
}
# The method names with the best mean of a column.
best <- function(column, bool_low = TRUE, num = 1, among = method_vec){
  value_vec <- avg(column)[among]
  names(sort(value_vec, decreasing = !bool_low))[seq_len(num)]
}
# A methods x splits table of chosen summary columns.
wide_table <- function(column_vec, label_vec, digits = 2,
                       among = method_vec){
  out_df <- data.frame(method = among, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  for(idx in seq_along(column_vec)){
    for(split in split_vec){
      out_df[[paste0(label_vec[idx], ", ", split)]] <-
        sapply(among, function(method){sm(method, column_vec[idx], split)})
    }
  }
  out_df$method <- paste0("`", out_df$method, "`")
  knitr::kable(out_df, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE)
}
num_genes <- ag("stored", "all", "num_genes", "split1")
# One number of the table of eSVD-DE's calls.
cl <- function(group, column, split){
  calls_df[calls_df$group == group & calls_df$split == split, column]
}
cl_both <- function(group, column, bool_pct = TRUE, digits = 2){
  value_vec <- sapply(split_vec, function(split){cl(group, column, split)})
  text_vec <- if(bool_pct) pct(value_vec) else fmt(value_vec, digits)
  paste0(text_vec[1], " and ", text_vec[2])
}
ag_both <- function(method, gene_set, column, digits = 2){
  value_vec <- sapply(split_vec, function(split){
    ag(method, gene_set, column, split)
  })
  paste0(fmt(value_vec[1], digits), " and ", fmt(value_vec[2], digits))
}
# Method names as inline code, comma separated. A backtick cannot be typed
# inside an inline chunk.
tick <- function(name_vec){
  paste0(intToUtf8(96), name_vec, intToUtf8(96), collapse = ", ")
}
state_vec <- grep("^state_adjusted", method_vec, value = TRUE)
keep_vec <- setdiff(method_vec, state_vec)
```

# Overview

This document is built from Kevin's note of 2026-11-15
(`2026-11-15_autoresearch-gabitto-replicate.txt`), from the two
autoresearch loops on the reported log fold change and its standard error
and the study that followed them
(`2026-11-12_autoresearch_beyond-score_claude.Rmd`), from Tati's Writeup45
fit of the Gabitto cohort (the design), and from Writeup49 (the split-half
and winner's-curse conventions). Everything before this document was
scored on simulated cohorts with a known truth. Here the Gabitto microglia
are split into two halves that share no donor, each half is fitted by
eSVD-DE on its own, and every rule is asked how well its logFC and SE from
one half agree with those from the other. The split is done twice.

**The question.** On a real cohort, which rule's log2 fold change and SE
replicate best between two independent halves: by the replicate analogue
of the autoresearch score, by the correlation of the logFC over the genes
that at least one half nominates as differentially expressed, and by
whether a nominated gene keeps the sign of its logFC in the other half?

What the document argues:

1. **The four fits are comparable and each took under 45 minutes.** Each
   half has 40 donors (13 or 14 controls) and about 20,000 nuclei; the
   package's test calls `r min(fit_df$num_esvd_deg)` to
   `r max(fit_df$num_esvd_deg)` genes per half at 5% FDR, and pseudobulk
   DESeq2 calls `r min(fit_df$num_deseq2_deg)` to
   `r max(fit_df$num_deseq2_deg)` (section 2.1).
2. **`state_adjusted` has the lowest replicate score and its logFC do not
   replicate.** Its score is `r both("state_adjusted", "all_score")` nats
   per gene, well below every other rule, while its two halves correlate at
   `r both("state_adjusted", "all_pearson")` and a gene nominated by
   eSVD-DE's test keeps its sign in the other half
   `r both("state_adjusted", "esvd_sign_rep", bool_pct = TRUE)` of the
   time. The rule's logFC have half the spread of the other rules' and an
   SE that matches that spread, which a score without a truth rewards
   (section 4.1).
3. **Among the rules that keep a signal, the `donor_wls` family has the
   lowest score in both splits**, `r both("donor_wls@esvd_nofloor", "all_score")`
   for `donor_wls@esvd_nofloor` against `r both("deseq2", "all_score")`
   for `deseq2` and `r both("stored", "all_score")` for `stored`, and it is
   also first on the score against the other half's DESeq2 (section 4.2).
4. **On the genes eSVD-DE's test nominates, the `donor_wls` family and the
   `raw` family correlate best between the halves** (`donor_wls`:
   `r both("donor_wls", "esvd_pearson")`; `raw`:
   `r both("raw", "esvd_pearson")`; `stored`:
   `r both("stored", "esvd_pearson")`; `deseq2`:
   `r both("deseq2", "esvd_pearson")`), and `donor_wls` is the more stable
   of the two across the splits (section 4.3).
5. **The SE of `stored` is about 2.5 times the disagreement between the
   halves, and the SE of `donor_wls` is about 10% above it** (`z_rms`
   `r both("stored", "all_z_rms")` and
   `r both("donor_wls@esvd_nofloor", "all_z_rms")`; 1 is calibrated). `raw`
   and `deseq2` are closest to 1, and `null_rescaled` is too small for the
   genes whose nuisance rate is at the cap (section 4.4).
6. **A gene that eSVD-DE's test calls in one half keeps the sign of its
   logFC in the other half `r cl_both("all calls", "sign_rep")` of the time
   in the two splits**, whichever rule supplies the logFC. The calls that
   change sign are concentrated among the genes at the nuisance cap and
   among the calls that `donor_wls` does not support at nominal
   $p < 0.05$, clearly in the second split and weakly in the first
   (section 4.5).
7. **The recommendation of the beyond-score study stands on real data**:
   report the pair from `donor_wls@esvd_nofloor`, do not use
   `state_adjusted` at the default rank on a cohort of this size, and read
   an eSVD-DE call together with the `donor_wls` interval. The bank needs
   examples where the rank is close to the number of donors, and the
   scorer needs a gate on retained signal (section 5).

*How to read.* The blue box says how the cohort was split; green boxes
close each results subsection with what it changes; the orange box in
section 5 is the procedure. A reader of the boxes alone has the argument.

| Stage | What it does | Section |
|---|---|---|
| Definitions | the cohort, the two splits, the four fits, the rules, the statistics | 2 |
| Each rule | the two halves against each other, one subsection per rule | 3 |
| Side by side | the score, the correlation, the SE, the sign of the nominated genes | 4 |
| Recommendation | the rule to report from and what the bank should add | 5 |

# Definitions

## The cohort and the two splits

The data are the microglia of the SEA-AD cohort of Gabitto et al. (2024)
as cleaned for the Was2CoDE analysis
(`Writeup43_gabitto_cleaned_only-counts.RData`):
`r format(sum(donor_df$num_cells), big.mark = ",")` nuclei of
`r nrow(donor_df)` donors and 5,256 genes. A donor is a case when
`CERAD_binary` is `Case`
(`r sum(donor_df$CERAD_binary == "Case")` donors) and a control otherwise
(`r sum(donor_df$CERAD_binary == "Control")` donors), the definition of
Tati's Writeup45 fit of the whole cohort.

::: {.generator}
The `r nrow(donor_df)` donors fall into eight strata of CERAD arm, sex and
APOE4 status. Within each stratum the donors are permuted and dealt
alternately to two halves, and the half that receives the first donor
alternates over the strata with an odd count so that the leftover donors
do not all land in one half. A donor is therefore in exactly one half of a
split. The procedure is run twice with different seeds (`split1`, seed 10;
`split2`, seed 20), and
`r sum(donor_df$split1 == donor_df$split2)` of the `r nrow(donor_df)`
donors keep their half label between the two splits. Each of the four
halves is then fitted on its own with `eSVD2::eSVD_helper()` of
version 1.2.0 at the settings of Writeup45: `k = 30`, covariates `sex`,
`APOE4status`, `PMI` and `Ageatdeath`, every other argument at its
default.
:::

```{r tab_balance}
knitr::kable(balance_df, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Table 1. The donors of each half, by arm. PMI and age at death were not stratified on.")
```

```{r tab_fits}
show_df <- fit_df[, c("fit", "num_case", "num_control", "num_cells",
                      "num_genes", "fit_minutes", "null_mean", "null_sd",
                      "share_capped", "num_esvd_deg", "num_deseq2_deg")]
knitr::kable(show_df, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Table 2. The four fits. `null_mean` and `null_sd` are the empirical null of the package's test; `share_capped` is the share of genes whose nuisance rate sits at the cap; the last two columns count the genes called at 5% FDR by the package's test and by pseudobulk DESeq2.")
```

## The rules

Every rule is the file the loops left, unedited, applied as in the
beyond-score study (`2026-11-12_autoresearch_beyond-score_claude.Rmd`,
section 2.2).

| Name in the tables | Rule | Reads of the fit |
|---|---|---|
| `stored` | what 1.2.0 reports: log ratio of the arms' mean posterior, SE from the posterior's mixture variances | posterior |
| `null_rescaled` | `stored`, the logFC shifted by the empirical null's mean and the SE multiplied by its SD | posterior, empirical null |
| `deshrunk` | `stored`'s logFC; between-donor SE of the posterior donor means divided by the shrinkage weight | posterior, library, nuisance rate |
| `raw` | ratio of the arms' means of donor means of $A/\ell$, delta-method SE between donors | library |
| `raw_null` | `raw` with the empirical null's shift and rescaling | library |
| `donor_wls` | weighted regression of $\log\{(y_{dg} + 1/2)/L_{dg}\}$ on the arm and the donor-level covariates, residual variance moderated across genes, logFC shifted by the null's mean | library |
| `gap_trend` | as `donor_wls` with voom-style weights and a variance trend in a covariate that contains the between-arm gap | library |
| `embed_prior` | `donor_wls` with the embedding's predicted donor variance in the moderation prior | library, embedding |
| `state_adjusted` | `donor_wls` on summaries with the embedding's donor offset removed; the arm coefficients' component along the loadings subtracted | library, embedding |
| `deseq2` | DESeq2 on donor pseudobulk; design: sex, APOE4 status, PMI, age at death and the arm | nothing |

Here $y_{dg}$ is the donor's summed count and $L_{dg}$ its summed library.
A suffix names the library a library-reading rule was handed in place of
the fitted one: `@esvd_nofloor` (the fitted library before the posterior's
floor at 0.1), `@esvd_depth` (the fitted intercept and depth alone),
`@total` (the cell's summed counts), `@sf` and `@tmm` (summed counts
rescaled to DESeq2's size factors or edgeR's TMM factors of the donor
pseudobulk). Every covariate of this design is constant within a donor,
so the `_cov` variants of the beyond-score study coincide with the plain
ones. `raw@esvd_nofloor` and `raw@total` were added on 2026-11-16 for the
Green study (`../2026-11-16_green/`), which compares `raw` and
`donor_wls` on one library; they appear in the tables and figures of
section 4 and no number of the other methods changed.

## What is compared between the two halves

For one rule and one split, gene $g$ has the pair
$(\widehat{\beta}_{g1}, s_{g1})$ from half 1 and
$(\widehat{\beta}_{g2}, s_{g2})$ from half 2, on the $\log_2$ scale. The
two halves share no donor, so the two estimates are independent given the
population's effect.

**The replicate score.** The autoresearch score is the Gaussian negative
log-likelihood of the true effect under $N(\widehat{\beta}_g, s_g^2)$. A
real cohort has no known truth, and the other half takes its place: if
both halves estimate one effect and both SEs are honest, the difference
$\widehat{\beta}_{g1} - \widehat{\beta}_{g2}$ is
$N(0, s_{g1}^2 + s_{g2}^2)$, and the score is

$$
\text{score} = \frac{1}{p}\sum_{g=1}^{p}
\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\log\{2\pi (s_{g1}^2 + s_{g2}^2)\} +
\frac{(\widehat{\beta}_{g1} - \widehat{\beta}_{g2})^2}{2 (s_{g1}^2 + s_{g2}^2)}\right],
$$

in nats per gene, lower being better. It rewards estimates that agree and
SEs that match the size of the disagreement. The companion calibration
number is the root mean square of
$(\widehat{\beta}_{g1} - \widehat{\beta}_{g2}) / \sqrt{s_{g1}^2 + s_{g2}^2}$
(`z_rms`), which is 1 when the SEs explain the disagreement and above 1
when they are too small. The replicate score differs from the autoresearch
score in one respect that matters for reading it: a bias that the two
halves share (a depth artifact, shrinkage toward a common value) cancels
in the difference, so the replicate score cannot see it.

**The score against a common target.** To give every rule the same
target, each rule's pair from one half is also scored against the *other*
half's pseudobulk DESeq2 estimate, the difference having variance
$s_{g}^2$ plus DESeq2's squared SE, averaged over the two directions
(`score_cross`). A rule cannot lower this number through a bias its own
two halves share, and the comparison favours DESeq2's estimand (the
marginal effect on summed counts).

**Nominated genes.** A gene is nominated when it is called at 5% FDR in at
least one half, under three definitions: by eSVD-DE's own test (the
package's `fdr_vec`; the same genes for every rule), by pseudobulk DESeq2
(`padj`; the same genes for every rule), and by the rule's own Wald test,
$z = \widehat{\beta}_g / s_g$ against the standard normal with BH over the
half's genes (a different gene set per rule, whose size is reported).

**Statistics on the nominated genes.** The Pearson correlation of
$\widehat{\beta}_{g1}$ and $\widehat{\beta}_{g2}$ over the nominated
genes; the share of discoveries whose logFC has the same sign in the
other half (`sign_rep`, each discovery counted from its discovering half);
and the replication slope (`slope_rep`), the least-squares line through
the origin of the replication half's logFC on the discovering half's, the
convention of Writeup49. A slope of 1 means the discovered effects
reappear at full size, and the winner's curse puts it below 1.

# Each rule between the two halves

Each subsection shows one rule. The upper figure has every gene, coloured
by the half whose Wald test of the rule's own pair nominates it; the lower
figure has only the genes that eSVD-DE's test nominates in at least one
half, the same genes in every subsection. The dashed line is the diagonal,
and a gene beyond the axes is drawn on the edge.

```{r per_method, results='asis', fig.width=8, fig.height=4.8}
.panel_labels <- function(method, gene_set, nomination){
  do.call(rbind, lapply(split_vec, function(split){
    discovery_row <- discovery_df[discovery_df$split == split &
                                    discovery_df$method == method &
                                    discovery_df$nomination == nomination, ]
    data.frame(split = split,
               label = paste0(ag(method, gene_set, "num_genes", split),
                              " nominated genes\n",
                              "r = ", fmt(ag(method, gene_set, "pearson",
                                             split)),
                              ", same sign in the other half ",
                              pct(discovery_row$sign_rep), "\n",
                              "replication slope ",
                              fmt(discovery_row$slope_rep)),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }))
}
.method_table <- function(method){
  out_df <- data.frame(
    split = split_vec,
    score = sapply(split_vec, function(s){sm(method, "all_score", s)}),
    z_rms = sapply(split_vec, function(s){sm(method, "all_z_rms", s)}),
    r_all = sapply(split_vec, function(s){sm(method, "all_pearson", s)}),
    score_cross = sapply(split_vec, function(s){sm(method, "score_cross", s)}),
    own_genes = sapply(split_vec, function(s){sm(method, "own_num_genes", s)}),
    own_both = sapply(split_vec, function(s){sm(method, "own_num_both", s)}),
    own_r = sapply(split_vec, function(s){sm(method, "own_pearson", s)}),
    own_sign = sapply(split_vec, function(s){sm(method, "own_sign_rep", s)}),
    own_slope = sapply(split_vec, function(s){sm(method, "own_slope_rep", s)}),
    esvd_r = sapply(split_vec, function(s){sm(method, "esvd_pearson", s)}),
    esvd_sign = sapply(split_vec, function(s){sm(method, "esvd_sign_rep", s)}),
    esvd_slope = sapply(split_vec, function(s){sm(method, "esvd_slope_rep", s)}),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  knitr::kable(out_df, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
}
for(method in section_vec){
  cat("\n\n## `", method, "`\n\n", sep = "")
  sub_df <- pair_df[pair_df$method == method, ]
  cat("Over all ", num_genes, " genes the replicate score of `", method,
      "` is ", both(method, "all_score"), " nats per gene in the two splits",
      " with `z_rms` ", both(method, "all_z_rms"),
      ", and the two halves' logFC correlate at ",
      both(method, "all_pearson"), ". Its own Wald test nominates ",
      sm(method, "own_num_genes", "split1"), " and ",
      sm(method, "own_num_genes", "split2"),
      " genes in at least one half, of which ",
      sm(method, "own_num_both", "split1"), " and ",
      sm(method, "own_num_both", "split2"), " in both halves.\n\n", sep = "")
  sub_df$nomination <- .nomination_factor(sub_df$own1, sub_df$own2)
  plot1 <- .plot_replication(
    plot_df = sub_df,
    label_df = .panel_labels(method, "nominated_own", "own"),
    title = paste0(method, ": all genes, coloured by the rule's own Wald ",
                   "test (BH 5%)"),
    bool_only_nominated = FALSE
  )
  plot(plot1)
  cat("\n\n")
  sub_df$nomination <- .nomination_factor(sub_df$esvd1, sub_df$esvd2)
  plot1 <- .plot_replication(
    plot_df = sub_df,
    label_df = .panel_labels(method, "nominated_esvd", "esvd"),
    title = paste0(method, ": genes nominated by eSVD-DE's test (FDR 5%) in ",
                   "at least one half"),
    bool_only_nominated = TRUE
  )
  plot(plot1)
  cat("\n\n")
  print(.method_table(method))
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

In each table, `score`, `z_rms` and `r_all` are over all genes; the
`own_` columns are over the genes the rule's own test nominates
(`own_genes` in at least one half, `own_both` in both); the `esvd_`
columns are over the genes eSVD-DE's test nominates.

# All rules side by side

```{r tab_summary}
wide_table(c("all_score", "score_cross", "all_z_rms", "all_pearson",
             "esvd_pearson", "esvd_sign_rep"),
           c("score", "score_cross", "z_rms", "corr_all", "corr_nominated",
             "sign_rep"))
```

Table 3. Every method in the two splits. `score`, `z_rms` and `corr_all` are
over all `r num_genes` genes; `corr_nominated` and `sign_rep` are over the
genes eSVD-DE's test nominates in at least one half
(`r sm("stored", "esvd_num_genes", "split1")` and
`r sm("stored", "esvd_num_genes", "split2")` genes).

## The replicate score alone ranks `state_adjusted` first, and its logFC do not replicate

```{r fig_score, fig.width=7, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="Figure 1. The replicate score of every method over all genes, one point per split."}
plot1 <- .plot_summary(summary_df, "all_score",
                       "Replicate score over all genes (nats per gene, lower is better)",
                       method_vec)
plot(plot1)
```

The three `state_adjusted` variants score `r fmt(min(avg("all_score")[state_vec]))`
to `r fmt(max(avg("all_score")[state_vec]))` nats per gene on average over
the two splits, and the best of the other methods scores
`r fmt(min(avg("all_score")[keep_vec]))`. The same rule's two halves
correlate at `r both("state_adjusted", "all_pearson")` over all genes and
at `r both("state_adjusted", "esvd_pearson")` over the genes eSVD-DE's test
nominates, and the sign of a nominated gene holds in the other half
`r both("state_adjusted", "esvd_sign_rep", bool_pct = TRUE)` of the time,
which is the rate of a coin. Its own Wald test nominates
`r sm("state_adjusted", "own_num_genes", "split1")` and
`r sm("state_adjusted", "own_num_genes", "split2")` genes, none of them in
both halves.

The score is low because the rule's logFC are small and its SE says so.
The SD of its logFC across genes is
`r ag_both("state_adjusted", "all", "sd_lfc")` against
`r ag_both("donor_wls", "all", "sd_lfc")` for `donor_wls`, the root mean
square difference between the halves is
`r ag_both("state_adjusted", "all", "rmsd")` against
`r ag_both("donor_wls", "all", "rmsd")`, and its `z_rms` is
`r both("state_adjusted", "all_z_rms")`. A pair of estimates that are
noise around zero with an honest SE satisfies the model behind the
replicate score exactly, and a truth-free score cannot separate that from
an accurate estimate of a small effect. The score against the other
half's DESeq2 does separate them: there `state_adjusted` scores
`r both("state_adjusted", "score_cross")` against
`r both("donor_wls", "score_cross")` for `donor_wls`, because its logFC do
not predict an independent estimate of the marginal effect
(correlation `r both("state_adjusted", "pearson_cross")` against
`r both("donor_wls", "pearson_cross")`).

The rule subtracts from each gene's arm coefficient its component along
the fitted loadings, and the fit here has rank 30 with 40 donors per half.
An embedding of that rank can carry most donor-level contrasts, the arm
contrast among them, so the subtraction removes the effect together with
the cell-state shift. The second loop's bank was fitted at rank 5, and its
report listed the rank as untested (open item 0C of `CLAUDE_kevin.md`).
The target of `state_adjusted` is the effect at fixed cell state, which
may be smaller than the marginal effect; a real effect at fixed cell
state would still have the same sign in two halves, and the rule's logFC
show no such agreement.

::: {.takeaway}
On a real cohort the replicate score has to be read with the correlation
between the halves beside it. `state_adjusted` wins the score by reporting
logFC with half the spread of every other rule and no agreement between
halves, so at rank 30 and 40 donors it has removed the case-control signal
and is not usable. It is left out of the rankings below.
:::

## Among the rules that keep a signal, the `donor_wls` family scores best

```{r fig_cross, fig.width=7, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="Figure 2. Each method's pair from one half scored against the other half's pseudobulk DESeq2 estimate, averaged over the two directions; one point per split."}
plot1 <- .plot_summary(summary_df, "score_cross",
                       "Score against the other half's DESeq2 (nats per gene, lower is better)",
                       method_vec)
plot(plot1)
```

Without `state_adjusted`, the lowest mean replicate score belongs to
`r tick(best("all_score", num = 3, among = keep_vec))`,
in that order, and the lowest mean score against the other half's DESeq2
to
`r tick(best("score_cross", num = 3, among = keep_vec))`.
`embed_prior` and `donor_wls` report the same logFC and differ by under
0.01 nats in either score, as on the simulated banks. `donor_wls@esvd_nofloor`
scores `r both("donor_wls@esvd_nofloor", "all_score")` in the two splits,
`deseq2` `r both("deseq2", "all_score")`, `raw` `r both("raw", "all_score")`,
`null_rescaled` `r both("null_rescaled", "all_score")` and `stored`
`r both("stored", "all_score")`. The ranking of `donor_wls` over `deseq2`
and of both over `stored` is the ranking of the three simulated banks.

**The library.** Removing the posterior's floor from the fitted library
improves `donor_wls` by
`r fmt(sm("donor_wls", "all_score", "split1") - sm("donor_wls@esvd_nofloor", "all_score", "split1"))`
and
`r fmt(sm("donor_wls", "all_score", "split2") - sm("donor_wls@esvd_nofloor", "all_score", "split2"))`
nats in the two splits, with the gain in the genes with 80% zeros or more
(Table 4). With the cell's summed counts as the library the score is
`r both("donor_wls@total", "all_score")`, behind the unfloored fitted
library in split 1 and equal to it in split 2, and the correlation between
the halves is slightly higher (`r both("donor_wls@total", "all_pearson")`
against `r both("donor_wls@esvd_nofloor", "all_pearson")`). Every
covariate of this design is constant within a donor, the setting in which
the beyond-score study found the fitted library and the summed counts
equivalent. `@esvd_depth` equals `@esvd_nofloor` to 0.005 nats, so the
fitted library's covariate columns add nothing here either.

```{r tab_sparsity}
strata_method_vec <- c("stored", "null_rescaled", "raw", "donor_wls",
                       "donor_wls@esvd_nofloor", "donor_wls@total", "deseq2")
set_vec <- c(zeros_below_80 = "under 80% zeros",
             zeros_80_to_95 = "80 to 95% zeros",
             zeros_above_95 = "over 95% zeros",
             rate_estimated = "rate estimated", rate_capped = "rate at the cap")
out_df <- data.frame(method = paste0("`", strata_method_vec, "`"),
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
for(gene_set in names(set_vec)){
  out_df[[set_vec[[gene_set]]]] <- sapply(strata_method_vec, function(method){
    mean(sapply(split_vec, function(split){
      ag(method, gene_set, "score", split)
    }))
  })
}
count_vec <- sapply(names(set_vec), function(gene_set){
  ag("stored", gene_set, "num_genes", "split1")
})
knitr::kable(out_df, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = paste0("Table 4. The replicate score by gene stratum, mean of the two splits. Genes per stratum in split 1: ", paste0(set_vec, " ", count_vec, collapse = "; "), "."))
```

::: {.takeaway}
The order of the simulated banks holds on Gabitto: `donor_wls` ahead of
pseudobulk DESeq2, both far ahead of `stored`, and the unfloored fitted
library at least as good as the floored one. The fitted library is not
better than summed counts on this cohort, whose covariates are all
donor-level.
:::

## Correlation over the nominated genes

```{r fig_nominated, fig.width=7, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="Figure 3. Correlation of the two halves' logFC over the genes that eSVD-DE's test nominates in at least one half (the same genes for every method); one point per split."}
plot1 <- .plot_summary(summary_df, "esvd_pearson",
                       "Correlation between the halves, genes nominated by eSVD-DE's test",
                       method_vec)
plot(plot1)
```

Over the genes eSVD-DE's test nominates, the highest mean correlation
between the halves belongs to
`r tick(best("esvd_pearson", bool_low = FALSE, num = 4, among = keep_vec))`.
The two splits disagree on the order of the families: `raw` leads in
split 1 (`r fmt(sm("raw", "esvd_pearson", "split1"))` against
`r fmt(sm("donor_wls", "esvd_pearson", "split1"))` for `donor_wls`) and
`donor_wls` in split 2 (`r fmt(sm("donor_wls", "esvd_pearson", "split2"))`
against `r fmt(sm("raw", "esvd_pearson", "split2"))`). `stored`
(`r both("stored", "esvd_pearson")`) is below both in each split, and
`deseq2` (`r both("deseq2", "esvd_pearson")`) is below `donor_wls` in
each split and above `raw` in split 2. Over
the `r sm("stored", "deseq2_num_genes", "split1")` and
`r sm("stored", "deseq2_num_genes", "split2")` genes DESeq2 nominates,
`donor_wls` is again the highest of the three (`donor_wls` `r both("donor_wls", "deseq2_pearson")`,
`stored` `r both("stored", "deseq2_pearson")`, `deseq2`
`r both("deseq2", "deseq2_pearson")`).

```{r tab_own}
wide_table(c("own_num_half1", "own_num_half2", "own_num_both", "own_sign_rep",
             "own_slope_rep"),
           c("half 1", "half 2", "both", "sign_rep", "slope_rep"),
           among = c("null_rescaled", "raw", "raw_null", "donor_wls",
                     "donor_wls@esvd_nofloor", "donor_wls@total", "gap_trend",
                     "embed_prior", "deseq2"))
```

Table 5. Each rule's own nominations (BH 5% on its Wald test): genes
nominated per half and in both, the share of discoveries with the same
sign in the other half, and the replication slope. A blank is fewer than
five discoveries.

A correlation over a rule's own nominations exists for few rules, because
with 13 or 14 controls per half the calibrated rules nominate almost
nothing: `donor_wls` `r sm("donor_wls", "own_num_genes", "split1")` and
`r sm("donor_wls", "own_num_genes", "split2")` genes, `deseq2`
`r sm("deseq2", "own_num_genes", "split1")` and
`r sm("deseq2", "own_num_genes", "split2")`. The rules that nominate many
are `null_rescaled` (`r sm("null_rescaled", "own_num_genes", "split1")`
and `r sm("null_rescaled", "own_num_genes", "split2")` genes, sign kept
`r both("null_rescaled", "own_sign_rep", bool_pct = TRUE)`), whose SE is
too small, `raw` (sign kept `r both("raw", "own_sign_rep", bool_pct = TRUE)`)
and `gap_trend` (`r sm("gap_trend", "own_num_genes", "split1")` and
`r sm("gap_trend", "own_num_genes", "split2")` genes, sign kept
`r both("gap_trend", "own_sign_rep", bool_pct = TRUE)`), whose SE the
first loop found to depend on the estimated effect. Where a calibrated
rule nominates five genes or more, the sign holds in at least
`r pct(min(summary_df$own_sign_rep[summary_df$method %in% c("donor_wls", "donor_wls@total", "donor_wls@sf", "donor_wls@tmm", "embed_prior@total")], na.rm = TRUE))`
of them.

::: {.takeaway}
On the genes nominated by eSVD-DE's test, `donor_wls` and its variants
replicate better than the posterior-based `stored` and better than DESeq2
in both splits. `raw` is first in one split and behind both `donor_wls`
and DESeq2 in the other.
:::

## The SE against the disagreement between the halves

```{r fig_zrms, fig.width=7, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="Figure 4. Root mean square of the standardized difference between the halves; 1 (dashed) means the SEs explain the disagreement, below 1 that they are too large."}
plot1 <- .plot_summary(summary_df, "all_z_rms",
                       "RMS of (lfc1 - lfc2) / sqrt(se1^2 + se2^2)",
                       method_vec, reference = 1)
plot(plot1)
```

The `stored` SE gives a `z_rms` of `r both("stored", "all_z_rms")`, so it
is `r fmt(1 / sm("stored", "all_z_rms", "split1"), 1)` and
`r fmt(1 / sm("stored", "all_z_rms", "split2"), 1)` times the SE that
would explain the disagreement between the halves, the same direction as
the 3.4 to 5 measured against simulated replicate cohorts in the SE
exploration and a smaller factor. `deshrunk`
is as wide (`r both("deshrunk", "all_z_rms")`). `null_rescaled` is at
`r both("null_rescaled", "all_z_rms")` over all genes and at
`r ag_both("null_rescaled", "rate_capped", "z_rms")` for the genes at the
nuisance cap, where its SE is too small. `raw` is at
`r both("raw", "all_z_rms")` and `deseq2` at `r both("deseq2", "all_z_rms")`.
`donor_wls@esvd_nofloor` is at `r both("donor_wls@esvd_nofloor", "all_z_rms")`,
an SE about 10 to 15% larger than the disagreement requires. A shared
true effect that differs between the halves' donors would push `z_rms`
above 1, so a value below 1 is an SE that is too large and not an
artifact of the split.

::: {.takeaway}
The stored SE is about 2.5 times too large on real data as well, and no
rescaling by the empirical null repairs it for the capped genes.
`donor_wls` errs on the conservative side by roughly a tenth.
:::

## Does a nominated gene keep its sign in the other half?

```{r fig_sign, fig.width=7, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="Figure 5. Share of the genes called by eSVD-DE's test in one half whose logFC, under each method, has the same sign in the other half; one point per split."}
plot1 <- .plot_summary(summary_df, "esvd_sign_rep",
                       "Same sign in the other half, genes nominated by eSVD-DE's test",
                       method_vec, reference = 0.5)
plot(plot1)
```

```{r tab_calls}
show_df <- calls_df[, c("split", "group", "num_calls", "sign_rep",
                        "sign_rep_wls", "slope_rep", "median_abs_lfc")]
knitr::kable(show_df, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Table 6. The genes eSVD-DE's test calls at 5% FDR in one half, by group. `sign_rep` uses the `stored` logFC of the two halves and `sign_rep_wls` that of `donor_wls@esvd_nofloor`; `slope_rep` is the replication slope of the `stored` logFC; the `donor_wls` p-value is the nominal Wald p of `donor_wls@esvd_nofloor` in the discovering half.")
```

Of the genes eSVD-DE's test calls in one half,
`r cl_both("all calls", "sign_rep")` have a `stored` logFC of the same
sign in the other half (Table 6), and every rule that keeps a signal is
between `r pct(min(summary_df$esvd_sign_rep[summary_df$method %in% keep_vec]))`
and `r pct(max(summary_df$esvd_sign_rep[summary_df$method %in% keep_vec]))`
(Figure 5). The rule that supplies the logFC therefore matters little for
the sign, and the calls matter more. A call whose gene has its nuisance
rate at the cap keeps its sign `r cl_both("rate at the cap", "sign_rep")`
of the time against `r cl_both("rate estimated", "sign_rep")` for the
other calls. A call that `donor_wls@esvd_nofloor` supports at nominal
$p < 0.05$ in the discovering half keeps its sign
`r cl_both("donor_wls p < 0.05", "sign_rep")` of the time
(`r cl_both("donor_wls p < 0.05", "sign_rep_wls")` under the rule's own
logFC) against `r cl_both("donor_wls p >= 0.05", "sign_rep")` for the
unsupported calls, and at $p < 0.01$ the share is
`r cl_both("donor_wls p < 0.01", "sign_rep_wls")` under the rule's logFC.
The replication slope of the calls is
`r cl_both("all calls", "slope_rep", bool_pct = FALSE)`: a called gene's
logFC reappears in the other half at a third to a half of its size, the
winner's curse that Writeup49 measured between cohorts.

A sign that flips is not by itself a false discovery, since a small true
effect estimated from 40 donors can change sign by chance. The share is
still informative as a bound: a null gene keeps its sign half the time,
so a sign agreement of $a$ among the calls allows at most $2(1 - a)$ of
them to be null, which is
`r pct(2 * (1 - cl("all calls", "sign_rep", "split1")))` and
`r pct(2 * (1 - cl("all calls", "sign_rep", "split2")))` here against a
nominal 5%. The beyond-score study measured a false discovery proportion
of 18 to 19% for the package's test on the two harder simulated banks.

::: {.takeaway}
The expectation that a nominated gene keeps its sign in the other half
holds for about four calls in five in one split and two in three in the
other, under any rule's logFC. In the second split the failures are
concentrated in the calls at the nuisance cap and the calls without
support from `donor_wls` in the discovering half, both of which keep
their sign about half the time; in the first split the differences have
the same direction and are small. A call with `donor_wls` $p < 0.01$
keeps its sign about nine times in ten in both.
:::

# Recommendation

**Which rule.** By the replicate score and the score against an
independent DESeq2 estimate, the `donor_wls` family is first among the
rules that retain a signal; by the correlation over nominated genes it is
in the leading group in both splits; its SE is within 15% of the
disagreement between the halves, on the conservative side. This is
a consequence of the evidence above and agrees with the three simulated
banks. Between the libraries, `@esvd_nofloor` is at least as good as the
floored library in both splits and is kept; summed counts would serve
equally on a cohort with donor-level covariates only, and the choice of
the fitted library rests on the simulated cell-level confounders, which
this cohort does not test.

**Which rule not.** `state_adjusted` is not usable at `k = 30` on 40
donors, and the replicate score must not be used alone to choose a rule
(a consequence). `stored` should not be the reported SE (a consequence,
third time measured). `raw` is a reasonable second, with an SE near 1 and
a less stable correlation across the two splits.

**How to read an eSVD-DE call.** Reporting, beside each call, whether the
`donor_wls@esvd_nofloor` interval excludes zero and whether the gene's
nuisance rate is at the cap identifies the calls that fail to keep their
sign (a choice, supported by Table 6 on two splits of one cohort).

::: {.recipe}
1. Fit the cohort with `eSVD2::eSVD_helper()` as now.
2. Rebuild the counts and the covariates of the fit and form the fitted
   library without the posterior's floor, the exponential of the fit's
   linear predictor over every covariate but the arm.
3. Report the log2 fold change and its SE from `donor_wls@esvd_nofloor`.
4. Beside each gene called by the package's test, report the Wald p-value
   of that pair and the nuisance status of the gene; treat a call with
   Wald $p \geq 0.05$ or a capped rate as provisional.
5. Check on a split of the cohort's donors, as here, that the rule's two
   halves correlate over the nominated genes. A rule whose halves do not
   correlate has no signal at this rank and donor count, whatever its
   score. If `state_adjusted` is wanted for the effect at fixed cell
   state, run this check first and lower the rank until it passes.
:::

**What the autoresearch bank should add.** Four things on this cohort
were outside what the banks could show.

1. *Rank close to the number of donors.* The second loop's bank was
   fitted at rank 5, and Gabitto's halves at rank 30 with 40 donors. A bank
   factor for the fitted rank (5, and a rank near the donor count) would
   have exposed `state_adjusted`.
2. *A gate on retained signal.* The scorer's gates are on the SE of
   strong-effect genes and on the slope of weak effects; a rule that
   returns noise around zero with a matching SE can pass a truth-free
   score. For banks with replicate cohorts (the third bank has them), a
   gate that the replicate correlation of the true DEGs stays above that
   of a reference rule would catch this failure, and on banks with a
   truth the slope of the logFC on the truth for strong effects serves
   the same purpose.
3. *Few controls and unbalanced arms.* The halves have 13 or 14 controls
   against 26 or 27 cases, and the banks' arms are balanced. Unbalanced
   examples would test the Welch degrees of freedom and the moderation of
   `donor_wls` where one arm is small.
4. *Weak, dense effects with a real share of capped genes.* Here 17% of
   genes are at the cap, the calibrated rules nominate almost nothing at
   40 donors, and the package's test nominates hundreds with a sign
   agreement that bounds its false discoveries at 38 to 69%. Examples
   with many small effects, a capped share of 15 to 20% and effects
   placed on capped genes would let the bank score the calls of each
   rule's Wald test (discoveries, false discovery proportion, sign
   errors) as well as the pair.

# What we glossed over

- **Two splits of one cohort.** The two splits share all 80 donors, and
  `r sum(donor_df$split1 == donor_df$split2)` donors have the same half
  label in both, so the splits are two looks at one data set and their
  agreement is not independent confirmation. Several orders differ
  between the splits (`raw` against `donor_wls` in section 4.3), and
  differences of under 0.02 nats or 0.05 in a correlation are within that
  variation. More splits would cost 40 minutes of fitting each.
- **Shared bias is invisible to a split.** A bias common to both halves
  (the depth adjustment, the half count for sparse genes, confounding by
  an unmeasured donor covariate) cancels in the difference and raises the
  correlation. The simulated banks, which have a truth, are the evidence
  against such a bias for `donor_wls`; the cross score against DESeq2 is
  a partial check here.
- **The rules' own tests use a normal reference.** `donor_wls` moderates
  its variance and has a $t$ reference with finite degrees of freedom,
  which would nominate slightly fewer genes still.
- **Each half has half the cohort's power.** The counts of nominated
  genes and the sign agreement describe cohorts of 40 donors, not the
  cohort of 80.
- **Assay is not adjusted for**, as in Writeup45 (two assays, `10x3v3`
  and `10xmultiome`), and neither split stratified on it, on PMI or on
  age at death (Table 1 shows the realized means).
- **The fits stopped after about 15 iterations per phase** at the default
  tolerance, which is why each took about 37 minutes against the 4 hours
  of the full cohort on the server. The loss decreased monotonically and
  no line-search warning was raised.
- **Why `state_adjusted` loses the signal was not dissected.** The rank
  explanation in section 4.1 is the mechanism the rule's construction
  suggests; a refit at a lower rank would test it.
- **The package's p-value was not recomputed.** Whether the test should
  follow the reported pair is open item 00A of `CLAUDE_kevin.md`.

# Files

All paths are relative to `additional_context/2026-11-15_gabitto/` unless
they start with `OUT`, which is `out/2026-11-15_gabitto/` beside the
repository clone (not in git).

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `paths_claude.R` | the data file, the output folder and the design shared by every step |
| `01_split-donors_claude.R` | the two stratified splits; writes `csv/split_donors.csv` (one row per donor), `csv/split_balance.csv` and `OUT/gabitto_splits.RData` |
| `02_fit-esvd_claude.R <label>` | one eSVD-DE fit; writes `OUT/gabitto_<label>_esvd.RData` (the diet `eSVD` object) |
| `03_apply-rules_claude.R <label>` | every rule, variant and DESeq2 on one fitted half; writes `OUT/gabitto_<label>_rules.RData` (genes x methods matrices of logFC and SE) |
| `04_evaluate_claude.R` | the comparisons; writes `OUT/gabitto_evaluation.RData`, `OUT/figures/*.png` and the tables below |
| `helpers_claude.R` | the replication statistics and the two figure functions, shared by step 4 and this document |
| `csv/fits.csv` | one row per fit |
| `csv/agreement.csv` | one row per split, method and gene set: score, `z_rms`, coverage, correlations, sign agreement |
| `csv/discovery.csv` | one row per split, method and nomination: discoveries per half, `sign_rep`, `slope_rep`, share replicated at nominal p < 0.05 |
| `csv/cross_score.csv` | one row per split and method: the score against the other half's DESeq2 |
| `csv/esvd_calls.csv` | one row per split and group of eSVD-DE's calls: number of calls, sign agreement, replication slope |
| `csv/summary.csv` | one row per split and method, the columns of the three tables above side by side |
| `csv/rule_runs.csv` | one row per fit and method: error message (empty when the rule ran) and seconds |
| `csv/gene_pairs.csv.gz` | one row per split, method and gene: the two halves' logFC and SE and the nominations; the figures of section 3 are drawn from it |
| `run_after-fits_claude.sh` | waits for the four fits, then runs step 3 on each and step 4 |
| `output/` | the logs of the four fits and of steps 3 and 4 |
